I've been farming this land since I was a teenager helping my mother. We've always grown wheat in the winter and corn in the summer — every family around us does the same. That's just how it's done here in Quzhou. The soil is flat, the wells are here, and the grain stations buy wheat and corn. I wouldn't know what to do with anything else, and neither would the buyers.

My family has about 8 mu. I'll plant all of it to wheat starting in October, and when I cut the wheat in June I'll turn right around and plant corn on the same fields. No time to waste.

For wheat seed, I'll buy from the village supply shop — they carry the improved varieties the county pushes. I don't save seed anymore because my neighbor told me yields dropped when she did that. For corn I'll get hybrid seed, same as last year — Zhengdan 958 or whatever the shop has, it always does well.

My father used to apply a lot of fertilizer and I do the same. I put down compound fertilizer before planting and then add urea when the wheat is jointing. For corn I mix in some urea when it's knee-high. I water the wheat three or four times — before winter sets in, again when it joints, and once more at heading. Corn I usually water twice unless there's good rain.

I spray pesticide when I see problems — aphids on wheat, or if there's rust. For corn I spray once or twice for borers. I plough before wheat planting and use the rotary tiller for corn since I'm in a hurry after harvest.

decision.reasoning_summary: I follow the winter wheat–summer maize double-cropping rotation standard in Quzhou County, Hebei, planting all 8 mu to wheat in October and immediately replanting to hybrid maize after the June harvest. Seed and input choices mirror what neighboring households and the village supply shop recommend, since I have no formal education and rely on local practice and family experience. Fertilizer rates are consistent with conventional smallholder norms in the region — higher nitrogen to protect yield — and irrigation follows the established schedule of four waterings for wheat and two for maize, drawing from groundwater wells. Tillage is conventional plough for wheat and rotary for maize to save time during the tight window between harvests.
